Our World: The week of Nov. 2, 2026
Our World is a roundup from our weekly print edition of noteworthy happenings, from our global correspondents and editors.
Success story for the Seychelles’ giant tortoises
Once hunted to near-extinction, giant tortoises now outnumber humans in the Seychelles, according to a recent survey reported by the Guardian. More than 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises now make their home in the uninhabited Aldabra Atoll, up from 100,000 in the 1990s and just 1,000 in the late 19th century. Today, giant tortoises can be found in only one other place in the wild: the Galápagos Islands, which have a much smaller population. Despite the progress, “the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species,” says Dave Hudson, a co-author of the study. – Ryan Lenora Brown 
Some BBC broadcasts suspended in Afghanistan
The Taliban have halted BBC FM-radio broadcasts inside Afghanistan. The British broadcaster had been the only international news organization still transmitting inside Afghanistan after two U.S. outlets were banned in 2022. Its FM programs reached 20% of the country’s adult population each week, according to BBC News. The Taliban said the FM transmissions had been suspended because of “repeated violations.” The BBC said it was continuing to report “fairly and independently” on short and medium wave, satellite and online. – Tim Backshall 
Central African Republic schools teaching Russian
As its isolation from the West grows, Russia has been cultivating states in Africa. Since 2017, about 1,500 Russian mercenaries, known as the Africa Corps, have been sent to bolster the Central African Republic regime of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra against attacks by a coalition of rebel groups. Seeking to supplement hard power with the soft variety, Moscow recently signed a deal with CAR to begin teaching Russian in three local schools from the sixth grade, as well as providing textbooks and teaching support, the independent news outlet Meduza reports. – Fred Weir
“A global benchmark for prison security”
That’s how Costa Rican President Laura Fernández characterized the opening of a new maximum security prison on Oct. 14 near the capital, San José. The prison can hold 5,100 inmates, which amounts to about one-fifth of the country’s prison population. Ms. Fernández is promising to usher in a new tough-on-crime approach, modeled after the harsh crackdown on drug gangs in El Salvador under President Nayib Bukele. Costa Rica has long been known as one of the safest countries in Latin America but has seen violent-crime rates rise in recent years. – Matthew Bell
